title: Chapter 6: Unemployment, Labor Market Structure, and Cyclical Slack
benchmark: Paul Krugman & Robin Wells, Macroeconomics (Principles SSOT, Spring 2027)

questions.title: Boundaries of the Civilian Noninstitutional Population (CNIP)
questions.prompt_template: Which of the following individuals is EXCLUDED from the U.S. Civilian Noninstitutional Population (CNIP) in the BLS Current Population Survey?

hints.text: Recall the three eligibility filters for the CNIP: age, military status, and institutional residence.
Full-time students and retirees aged 16 or older are still inside the CNIP (classified as NILF), whereas active-duty service members and institutionalized residents are excluded.

options_template.text: A 68-year-old retired engineer living in a private residence who is not looking for work.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (NILF-Exclusion Confusion): Retirees aged 16+ living outside institutions are included in the CNIP and partitioned into Not in the Labor Force (NILF).

options_template.text: A 19-year-old full-time college sophomore living in a campus dormitory with no paid job.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Student-Status Misclassification): Full-time college students aged 16+ are part of the CNIP; they are classified as NILF if neither working nor actively searching.

options_template.text: A 24-year-old active-duty U.S. Navy officer stationed at a domestic naval base.
options_template.feedback: Correct. The CNIP includes U.S. residents aged 16 and older who are neither on active military duty nor residing in institutions such as correctional facilities or nursing homes.

options_template.text: A 35-year-old discouraged worker who stopped applying for jobs six months ago.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Labor Force vs. CNIP Confusion): Discouraged workers are excluded from the labor force (placed in NILF), but they remain inside the Civilian Noninstitutional Population.

questions.title: Behavioral Threshold for Employed (E) Status
questions.prompt_template: Under BLS Current Population Survey (CPS) rules, which individual is classified as Employed (E) during the monthly reference week?

hints.text: The CPS uses objective behavioral thresholds for work hours, unpaid family enterprise hours, and temporary job attachment.
Working at least 1 hour for pay, working 15+ unpaid hours in a family business, or being temporarily absent from an existing job all qualify as Employed (E).

options_template.text: A salaried software developer who took two weeks of unpaid parental leave from her job and did not work during the reference week.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Individuals who hold a job from which they are temporarily absent due to illness, vacation, weather, industrial dispute, or parental leave are counted as Employed (E) in the CPS.

options_template.text: A college student who volunteered 20 unpaid hours at a local nonprofit animal shelter.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Volunteer Work Misclassification): Unpaid volunteer work at a nonprofit does not count as employment; only 15+ unpaid hours in a family-operated business qualify for E.

options_template.text: A teenager who worked 10 unpaid hours helping at her parents' bakery during the reference week.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Unpaid Family Hours Threshold Error): Unpaid work in a family-operated enterprise requires at least 15 hours during the reference week to be counted as Employed (E).

options_template.text: A recently laid-off machinist awaiting recall to his factory in three weeks.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Temporary Layoff Misclassification): Workers on temporary layoff awaiting recall are classified as Unemployed (U), not Employed (E), even without active job search.

questions.title: Three Simultaneous Conditions for Unemployed (U)
questions.prompt_template: Except for workers on temporary layoff awaiting recall, what three conditions must a person in the CNIP simultaneously satisfy to be counted as Unemployed (U) in the CPS?

hints.text: Think about current work status, readiness to start a job, and the specific time window for job search.
The CPS requires active job search within the preceding four weeks, not merely desiring a job or searching within the past year.

options_template.text: No full-time employment, registered for state unemployment insurance benefits, and actively searching within the past 12 months.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (UI-Registration Myth): Receiving or registering for unemployment insurance is NOT a CPS requirement for being counted in U, and the active search window is 4 weeks, not 12 months.

options_template.text: No employment during the reference week, currently available to start work, and engaged in active job search within the preceding four weeks.
options_template.feedback: Correct. To be counted in U, a respondent must have zero employment in the reference week, be available for work (except for temporary illness), and have actively searched within the past four weeks.

options_template.text: Working fewer than 20 hours per week, wanting full-time work, and actively applying within the past four weeks.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Part-Time Confusion): Anyone working even 1 hour for pay during the reference week is counted as Employed (E), not Unemployed (U); involuntary part-time workers are tracked separately in U-6.

options_template.text: No employment during the reference week, desiring a job, and reading online job postings within the past four weeks.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Passive Search Fallacy): Merely reading job postings without submitting applications, interviewing, or contacting employers is passive search and places the person in NILF.

questions.title: Distinguishing Active Job Search from Not in the Labor Force
questions.prompt_template: Carlos has no job and is available to work immediately. During the past four weeks, he browsed online job boards every morning to check salaries but did not submit any applications, contact employers, or attend interviews. How does the BLS classify Carlos?

hints.text: Check whether browsing job listings meets the CPS standard of 'active job search.'
Active search requires concrete steps that could result in a job offer (applying, interviewing, contacting employers).

options_template.text: Employed (E), because researching labor market wages is a productive economic activity.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Unpaid Search as Work): Job search is not paid employment or unpaid family business work, so Carlos cannot be classified as Employed (E).

options_template.text: Unemployed (U), because he wants a job and checked job postings within the past four weeks.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Passive Search Confusion): Simply browsing listings without contacting employers or submitting applications is passive search and does not satisfy the CPS active-search requirement.

options_template.text: Part-time for economic reasons (PT_econ), because he is available for full-time work but currently works zero hours.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Zero-Hours Misclassification): PT_econ applies only to employed individuals working between 1 and 34 hours per week who want full-time work.

options_template.text: Not in the Labor Force (NILF), because he did not engage in active job search within the preceding four weeks.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Because Carlos neither worked nor took active steps such as submitting applications or contacting employers in the past four weeks, the CPS classifies him as Not in the Labor Force (NILF).

questions.topic: CPS Household Survey vs. CES Establishment Survey
questions.title: Comparing the CPS Household Survey and CES Payroll Survey
questions.prompt_template: A freelance graphic designer works 25 hours a week as a self-employed contractor and also works 15 hours a week on the payroll of two different retail stores. How is this individual recorded across the CPS Household Survey and the CES Establishment Survey?

hints.text: Compare the sampling unit of each survey: person-based households (CPS) vs. nonfarm employer payrolls (CES).
Remember that the CES excludes self-employment and counts each payroll job separately.

options_template.text: Counted three times in CPS employment and once in CES nonfarm payrolls.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Survey Reversal): This reverses the two surveys; CPS is person-based (counts each employed individual once) while CES is job-based.

options_template.text: Counted once in CPS employment and three times in CES nonfarm payrolls.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Self-Employment Inclusion Error): The CES Establishment Survey excludes self-employed contractors, so the freelance role is not counted in CES payrolls.

options_template.text: Counted once in CPS employment and twice in CES nonfarm payrolls.
options_template.feedback: Correct. The CPS counts each employed person exactly once regardless of multiple jobs, whereas the CES excludes self-employment and records each of the two retail payroll positions separately.

options_template.text: Excluded from CPS employment because of self-employment, and counted twice in CES nonfarm payrolls.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (CPS Coverage Error): The CPS household survey explicitly includes self-employed, agricultural, and qualifying unpaid family workers in total employment (E).

questions.title: Relationship Between Discouraged Workers (D) and Marginally Attached Workers (M)
questions.prompt_template: How are Discouraged Workers (D) related to Marginally Attached Workers (M) in BLS labor underutilization statistics?

hints.text: Both groups are currently classified as NILF and searched for work within the past 12 months, though not in the past 4 weeks.
Focus on the specific reason cited for not searching recently: labor-market pessimism vs. non-market barriers like childcare.

options_template.text: Discouraged workers are a subset of marginally attached workers who cite labor-market reasons—such as believing no jobs are available—for not searching in the past four weeks.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Both D and M are NILF individuals who want work and searched within the past 12 months; D is the subset of M citing labor-market reasons, while other M workers cite barriers like childcare or transportation.

options_template.text: Marginally attached workers are a subset of discouraged workers who have been unemployed for more than 15 weeks.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Subset Inversion & U-1 Confusion): Discouraged workers (D) are a subset of marginally attached workers (M), not vice versa, and 15+ week joblessness defines U-1.

options_template.text: Discouraged workers and marginally attached workers are mutually exclusive groups that must both be added separately to U when computing U-6.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Double-Counting Fallacy): Because D is already contained inside M, adding both M and D to the U-6 numerator double-counts discouraged workers.

options_template.text: Discouraged workers are counted inside the official labor force (LF), whereas marginally attached workers are classified as NILF.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Labor Force Boundary Error): Neither D nor M searched actively in the past four weeks, so both groups are classified as NILF and excluded from LF.

questions.title: Defining Part-Time for Economic Reasons (PT_econ)
questions.prompt_template: Which worker is counted in 'Part-Time for Economic Reasons' (PT_econ) when constructing the BLS U-6 underutilization rate?

hints.text: Check both the weekly hour threshold (< 35 hours) and whether the part-time schedule is involuntary due to labor market conditions.
Workers who prefer part-time hours for school, caregiving, or semi-retirement are 'part-time for noneconomic reasons' and excluded from PT_econ.

options_template.text: A graduate student who voluntarily works 20 hours per week at a cafe so she can attend classes.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Voluntary Part-Time Inclusion): Students choosing part-time work to attend school are part-time for noneconomic reasons and are excluded from PT_econ and U-6.

options_template.text: A warehouse associate whose hours were cut from 40 to 24 per week due to slack business conditions, and who is available for full-time work.
options_template.feedback: Correct. PT_econ captures workers employed fewer than 35 hours per week who prefer and are available for full-time work but face reduced hours or inability to find a full-time role.

options_template.text: A retail manager working 45 hours per week who feels underpaid relative to her college degree.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Skills Mismatch vs. Hours Rationing): Although overqualification is a form of underemployment informally, BLS PT_econ strictly measures working fewer than 35 hours involuntarily.

options_template.text: A semi-retired accountant who works 18 hours per week by choice to supplement pension income.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Voluntary Part-Time Inclusion): Because this worker prefers a part-time schedule rather than seeking full-time hours, he is excluded from PT_econ.

questions.title: Comparing BLS Alternative Underutilization Measures (U-1 to U-6)
questions.prompt_template: Which BLS underutilization measure specifically adds all marginally attached workers (M) to the unemployed, but does NOT include involuntary part-time workers (PT_econ)?

hints.text: Trace the progression from narrowest (U-1) to broadest (U-6) in the BLS table.
U-3 is headline unemployment, U-4 adds discouraged workers (D), U-5 adds all marginally attached workers (M), and U-6 adds PT_econ.

options_template.text: U-2, defined as job losers and persons who completed temporary jobs as a percent of LF.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Narrow-Measure Confusion): U-2 is narrower than U-3 and measures only job losers within the official labor force, excluding NILF groups like M.

options_template.text: U-4, defined as (U + D) / (LF + D).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Subset Omission): U-4 adds only discouraged workers (D), omitting non-discouraged marginally attached workers (such as those facing childcare or transportation barriers).

options_template.text: U-5, defined as (U + M) / (LF + M).
options_template.feedback: Correct. U-5 expands U-3 by adding all marginally attached workers (M) to both numerator and denominator, stopping just short of adding involuntary part-time workers (which defines U-6).

options_template.text: U-6, defined as (U + M + PT_econ) / (LF + M).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Over-Inclusion Error): U-6 explicitly includes involuntary part-time workers (PT_econ) in its numerator alongside U and M.

questions.title: Why M Enters Both Numerator and Denominator of U-6 While PT_econ Enters Only the Numerator
questions.prompt_template: In the BLS formula U-6 = (U + M + PT_econ) / (LF + M) × 100, why is M added to the denominator while PT_econ is NOT added to the denominator?

hints.text: Ask where each group lives in the original BLS population partition: inside LF or inside NILF?
Every worker counted in the numerator of a percentage rate must also be counted exactly once in the denominator.

options_template.text: Because PT_econ workers are classified as NILF, whereas M workers are already counted inside Employed (E).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Category Inversion): This reverses the BLS partition—PT_econ workers are employed (inside E and LF), whereas M workers are inside NILF.

options_template.text: Because adding PT_econ to the denominator would make U-6 larger than 100% during deep recessions.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Algebraic Direction Error): Adding a positive number to the denominator shrinks a fraction; omitting PT_econ from the denominator avoids double-counting them, not exceeding 100%.

options_template.text: Because the BLS ignores involuntary part-time workers when measuring total labor supply.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Exclusion Fallacy): Involuntary part-time workers ARE in total labor supply—they are already counted inside E, which is part of LF = E + U.

options_template.text: Because PT_econ workers are already employed inside LF, whereas M workers are drawn from NILF and must be added to LF so the ratio stays a valid proportion of the expanded labor pool.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Since PT_econ ⊂ E ⊂ LF, adding PT_econ to the denominator would double-count them; since M ⊂ NILF, adding M to LF keeps U-6 consistently bounded between 0% and 100%.

questions.title: Economic Nature of Frictional Unemployment (u_f)
questions.prompt_template: Which scenario is the clearest example of frictional unemployment (u_f)?

hints.text: Frictional unemployment reflects normal, short-term search and matching between heterogeneous workers and available vacancies.
Distinguish voluntary career transitions or new entry from skill obsolescence, wage floors, or economy-wide recessions.

options_template.text: A coal miner loses his job after local mines close permanently and lacks the credentials required for nearby healthcare vacancies.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Structural Misclassification): Permanent industry decline and skill/credential mismatch generate structural unemployment (u_s), not frictional unemployment.

options_template.text: A marketing analyst resigns after relocating to a new city and spends five weeks interviewing for roles that match her experience.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Short-term unemployment arising from geographic relocation, imperfect information, and normal job-matching search is frictional unemployment (u_f).

options_template.text: An assembly-line worker is laid off when a nationwide recession causes automobile sales to plunge across all manufacturers.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Cyclical Misclassification): Job losses triggered by an economy-wide shortfall in aggregate demand represent cyclical unemployment (u_c).

options_template.text: Entry-level applicants remain unable to find work because a steep binding minimum wage holds real wages above market-clearing equilibrium.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Wage-Rigidity Misclassification): Persistent excess labor supply created by a binding wage floor is structural unemployment (u_s), not frictional search.

questions.title: Distinguishing Structural Unemployment (u_s) from Frictional Search
questions.prompt_template: What fundamentally distinguishes structural unemployment (u_s) from frictional unemployment (u_f)?

hints.text: Compare whether sufficient suitable jobs exist at the prevailing real wage.
In frictional unemployment, jobs exist and take time to match; in structural unemployment, mismatches or wage rigidities create a persistent shortage of jobs at prevailing wages.

options_template.text: Structurally unemployed workers face a persistent shortage of suitable jobs at prevailing wages due to skill/geographic mismatches or wage rigidities, whereas frictionally unemployed workers are in temporary search for available matches.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Structural unemployment persists because workers lack required skills/location or because real wages are held above equilibrium, leaving more job seekers than openings.

options_template.text: Structural unemployment occurs only during recessions, whereas frictional unemployment occurs only during economic booms.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Cyclical Confusion): Business-cycle fluctuations drive cyclical unemployment (u_c); both u_f and u_s are components of the natural rate (u*) present across all phases of the cycle.

options_template.text: Structural unemployment is excluded from the natural rate of unemployment (u*), whereas frictional unemployment is included.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Natural Rate Formula Error): By definition, the natural rate of unemployment equals the sum of frictional and structural unemployment (u* = u_f + u_s).

options_template.text: Structural unemployment is always voluntary and efficiency-enhancing, whereas frictional unemployment is caused exclusively by minimum wage laws.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Concept Reversal): Frictional search is typically short-term and efficiency-enhancing for match quality, whereas binding wage floors are a classic source of structural unemployment.

questions.topic: Natural Rate of Unemployment & Full Employment
questions.title: Meaning of 'Full Employment' and the Natural Rate (u* / NAIRU)
questions.prompt_template: In macroeconomics, what does it mean when an economy is operating at 'full employment'?

hints.text: Recall the decomposition u = u_f + u_s + u_c and the definition u* = u_f + u_s.
Full employment corresponds to zero cyclical slack and output equal to potential GDP (Y = Y*), not zero total joblessness.

options_template.text: The headline unemployment rate U-3 equals exactly 0.0% because every person in the labor force holds a job.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Zero-Unemployment Myth): Even at full capacity, dynamic labor markets always have positive frictional and structural unemployment (u_f + u_s > 0).

options_template.text: The labor force participation rate equals 100% and there are no individuals classified as NILF.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Participation Confusion): Full employment does not require retirees, students, or homemakers to enter the labor force; it is defined by u = u*.

options_template.text: Actual unemployment equals the natural rate (u = u*), cyclical unemployment is zero (u_c = 0), and real GDP equals potential output (Y = Y*).
options_template.feedback: Correct. Full employment means zero cyclical unemployment (u = u* = u_f + u_s), also called the NAIRU, at which the economy sustainably produces its potential real GDP (Y*).

options_template.text: Frictional and structural unemployment have both been eliminated, leaving only cyclical unemployment.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Component Reversal): Full employment eliminates cyclical unemployment (u_c = 0), while positive frictional and structural unemployment remain.

questions.title: Why Firms Voluntarily Pay Efficiency Wages Above Market Equilibrium
questions.prompt_template: Even in the complete absence of minimum wage laws or labor unions, why might profit-maximizing firms voluntarily pay real wages above the market-clearing equilibrium?

hints.text: Think about microeconomic incentives inside the firm: effort monitoring, turnover costs, and applicant quality.
In efficiency-wage theories (such as Shapiro–Stiglitz or Akerlof's gift-exchange), higher wages raise worker productivity or lower turnover costs.

options_template.text: To guarantee that cyclical unemployment falls to zero during macroeconomic recessions.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Macro-Goal Attribution): Individual firms set wages to maximize their own profits, not to stabilize aggregate cyclical unemployment; above-market wages actually raise structural unemployment.

options_template.text: To comply with BLS Current Population Survey reporting requirements for nonfarm establishments.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Institutional Confusion): The BLS collects labor statistics neutrally and does not mandate above-market wages.

options_template.text: Because labor supply curves are downward-sloping whenever real wages rise above equilibrium.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Slope Error): Labor supply slopes upward; efficiency wages operate through productivity, turnover, and effort incentives rather than an inverted supply curve.

options_template.text: To boost morale, reduce costly turnover, attract higher-ability applicants, and deter shirking when worker effort is costly to monitor.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Efficiency wages raise productivity and reduce hiring/training and monitoring costs enough to be profitable for firms, while generating above-equilibrium real wages and structural joblessness.

questions.title: Effect of College Graduates Entering Active Job Search (NILF → U)
questions.prompt_template: In the BLS population partition tree, suppose 1.0 million full-time college seniors graduate and immediately begin actively applying for jobs, moving from NILF to Unemployed (U) before receiving offers. Holding E and P constant, how do U-3, LFPR, and EPOP respond?

hints.text: Track which boxes in the BLS tree change: NILF falls by 1.0M, U rises by 1.0M, LF rises by 1.0M, while E and P stay fixed.
Adding the same positive number to both numerator and denominator of a fraction less than 1 strictly increases the fraction.

options_template.text: U-3 is unchanged, LFPR increases, and EPOP decreases.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Proportionality Fallacy): Adding 1.0M to both U and LF raises U/LF because U < LF, and EPOP = E/P does not change when E and P are constant.

options_template.text: U-3 increases, LFPR increases, and EPOP remains unchanged.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Moving graduates from NILF to U increases both U and LF by 1.0M (raising U-3 = U/LF and LFPR = LF/P), while E and P are unchanged so EPOP = E/P stays constant.

options_template.text: U-3 increases, LFPR remains unchanged, and EPOP decreases.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Labor Force Boundary Error): Moving from NILF into U expands the labor force (LF = E + U), so LFPR = LF/P must rise while EPOP = E/P stays unchanged.

options_template.text: U-3 decreases, LFPR increases, and EPOP increases.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Direction Reversal): New job seekers who have not yet been hired enter U, not E, so U-3 rises and EPOP does not increase.

questions.title: Effect of Discouraged Workers Exiting the Labor Force (U → NILF)
questions.prompt_template: During a prolonged downturn, 500,000 unemployed workers become discouraged and stop actively searching for jobs, moving from U into Marginally Attached (M) inside NILF while E and P remain constant. What happens to headline U-3, LFPR, and EPOP?

hints.text: Subtracting 500,000 from both U and LF shrinks the numerator proportionally faster than the denominator.
Check whether E or P changed at all during this transition.

options_template.text: Headline U-3 decreases, LFPR decreases, and EPOP remains unchanged.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Exiting from U to NILF reduces both U and LF by 500,000 (lowering U/LF and LF/P), while E and P are unaffected so EPOP = E/P remains constant.

options_template.text: Headline U-3 increases, LFPR decreases, and EPOP decreases.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Discouraged-Worker Direction Fallacy): Discouraged workers leave U rather than entering it, so headline U-3 falls artificially rather than rising, and EPOP is unaffected.

options_template.text: Headline U-3 remains unchanged, LFPR decreases, and EPOP remains unchanged.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Equal-Subtraction Fallacy): Subtracting the same positive amount from numerator and denominator of U/LF (where U < LF) strictly lowers the ratio rather than keeping it constant.

options_template.text: Headline U-3 decreases, LFPR remains unchanged, and EPOP increases.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Labor Force & Employment Confusion): Exiting into NILF reduces LF (lowering LFPR), and no jobs were created so EPOP cannot increase.

questions.title: Comparing U-3 and U-6 When Unemployed Workers Become Discouraged
questions.prompt_template: In the U-3 versus U-6 stacked bar diagram, suppose 1.5 million unemployed workers stop active search due to pessimism about job prospects and transition from U into Marginally Attached (M), while E and PT_econ stay fixed. How do the U-3 and U-6 rates respond?

hints.text: In U-6 = (U + M + PT_econ) / (LF + M), notice what happens to U + M and to LF + M = E + U + M.
A flow from U to M simply relabels workers within the existing U-6 numerator and denominator.

options_template.text: Both U-3 and U-6 decrease by the same number of percentage points.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Parallel-Movement Assumption): While U-3 drops because workers exit U and LF, U-6 retains those workers inside M in both numerator and denominator.

options_template.text: U-3 decreases while U-6 increases.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Double-Counting Intuition): Shifting workers from U to M reduces U by 1.5M and raises M by 1.5M, leaving U + M and LF + M completely unchanged.

options_template.text: U-3 decreases while U-6 remains completely unchanged.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Because the workers merely move from U to M, U-3 = U/LF falls, whereas both the U-6 numerator (U + M + PT_econ) and denominator (E + U + M) are completely unchanged.

options_template.text: U-3 remains unchanged while U-6 increases.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Denominator Neglect): Exiting active search removes workers from U and LF (lowering U-3), while leaving total U-6 sums unchanged.

questions.title: Intensive-Margin Recovery in the U-3 vs. U-6 Diagram
questions.prompt_template: As consumer demand strengthens, employers restore full-time 40-hour schedules to 2.0 million workers who were previously working part-time for economic reasons (PT_econ). Total employment (E), unemployment (U), and marginal attachment (M) do not change. How do U-3, U-6, and the (U-6 − U-3) spread respond?

hints.text: Check whether restoring full-time hours to an already-employed worker changes E, U, or LF.
Only the PT_econ segment of the U-6 numerator shrinks while its denominator (LF + M) stays fixed.

options_template.text: U-3 decreases, U-6 decreases, and the spread (U-6 − U-3) stays constant.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Extensive-Margin Confusion): Because PT_econ workers were already counted in E, converting them to full-time leaves E, U, and U-3 completely unchanged.

options_template.text: U-3 decreases, U-6 remains unchanged, and the spread widens.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Metric Reversal): U-3 ignores hours worked and stays unchanged, whereas U-6 directly captures the decline in PT_econ.

options_template.text: Both U-3 and U-6 remain unchanged because total employment (E) did not change.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Binary-Employment Fallacy): While U-3 treats 1 hour and 40 hours identically, U-6 specifically tracks intensive-margin work-hour recovery via PT_econ.

options_template.text: U-3 remains unchanged, U-6 decreases, and the spread (U-6 − U-3) narrows.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Because E, U, and LF are unchanged, U-3 stays constant; meanwhile PT_econ drops in the U-6 numerator (with LF + M fixed), lowering U-6 and compressing the spread.

questions.title: Identifying Structural Unemployment on the Aggregate Labor Market Graph
questions.prompt_template: In the aggregate labor market diagram with real wage (W/P) on the vertical axis and quantity of labor (L) on the horizontal axis, a binding real wage floor (W/P)_floor is imposed above the market-clearing real wage (W/P)*. How is the resulting structural unemployment represented graphically?

hints.text: At any real wage above equilibrium, compare the horizontal coordinates on the labor demand curve (L_D) and labor supply curve (L_S).
Structural unemployment equals the excess supply of labor at the binding wage floor.

options_template.text: The horizontal distance (L_S − L_D) between the labor supply and labor demand curves at (W/P)_floor.
options_template.feedback: Correct. At (W/P)_floor > (W/P)*, firms hire only L_D workers while L_S workers seek jobs, generating persistent structural unemployment equal to the horizontal surplus L_S − L_D.

options_template.text: The vertical distance (W/P)_floor − (W/P)* between the wage floor and the equilibrium real wage.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Axis Confusion): The vertical distance measures the real wage premium above equilibrium in dollars per hour, not the quantity of unemployed workers.

options_template.text: The horizontal distance (L* − L_D) between equilibrium employment and employment at the wage floor.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Partial-Surplus Error): L* − L_D measures only jobs lost relative to equilibrium; total structural unemployment also includes additional job seekers (L_S − L*) attracted by the higher wage.

options_template.text: The horizontal distance (L_S − L*) between labor supply at the wage floor and equilibrium employment.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Partial-Surplus Error): L_S − L* captures only new labor force entrants and omits the L* − L_D workers displaced as firms move up along L_D.

questions.title: Raising an Already-Binding Real Wage Floor
questions.prompt_template: Suppose an economy's labor market already operates with a binding real wage floor above (W/P)*. If policymakers raise the real wage floor even higher, what graphical movements occur along L_D and L_S?

hints.text: Does changing the wage floor shift the L_D and L_S curves, or cause movements along them?
Check what happens to quantity of labor demanded and quantity of labor supplied as (W/P) rises.

options_template.text: L_D shifts leftward and L_S shifts rightward, leaving structural unemployment ambiguous.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Shift vs. Movement Confusion): A change in the real wage itself causes movements along existing L_D and L_S curves, not shifts of the curves.

options_template.text: Firms move upward-left along L_D (reducing employment) and workers move upward-right along L_S (expanding labor supply), unambiguously widening structural unemployment (L_S − L_D).
options_template.feedback: Correct. Raising a binding wage floor moves both sides along their respective curves—cutting L_D and increasing L_S—which unambiguously widens the structural surplus L_S − L_D.

options_template.text: Firms move downward-right along L_D and workers move downward-left along L_S, narrowing structural unemployment.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Slope Inversion): Moving to a higher real wage reduces quantity demanded (upward-left along L_D) and raises quantity supplied (upward-right along L_S).

options_template.text: Employment stays fixed at L* while only L_S increases.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Inelastic Demand Assumption): Along a downward-sloping labor demand curve, a higher binding real wage reduces the quantity of labor firms hire.

questions.title: Graphical Outcome of a Non-Binding Minimum Wage
questions.prompt_template: In the aggregate labor market diagram, if the statutory minimum wage is set BELOW the market-clearing real wage (W/P)*, what is the resulting labor market outcome?

hints.text: A minimum wage sets a legal floor—employers may pay more than the floor, just not less.
Check whether the equilibrium wage (W/P)* already complies with the legal floor.

options_template.text: A persistent labor shortage equal to L_D − L_S at the minimum wage.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Price Ceiling Confusion): A wage floor below equilibrium does not prevent wages from rising to (W/P)*; shortages occur only under binding price ceilings.

options_template.text: Structural unemployment equal to L_S − L_D at the minimum wage.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Automatic-Binding Fallacy): A wage floor generates structural unemployment only when it is binding—that is, set strictly ABOVE (W/P)*.

options_template.text: The wage floor is non-binding, so the market clears at (W/P)* and L* with zero wage-floor structural unemployment.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Because the competitive real wage (W/P)* already exceeds the statutory floor, the law does not constrain wage setting and the market clears at (L*, (W/P)*).

options_template.text: The labor demand curve shifts rightward until (W/P)* falls to match the minimum wage.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Spurious Curve Shift): Setting a non-binding statutory floor does not alter worker productivity or shift labor demand.

questions.title: Leftward Labor Demand Shift Under a Rigid Real Wage
questions.prompt_template: Starting from a labor market with a binding real wage floor (W/P)_floor (such as a multi-year collective bargaining contract), suppose a negative demand shock shifts the labor demand curve L_D to the left while (W/P)_floor stays rigid. What happens graphically?

hints.text: Draw a leftward shift of L_D at the fixed horizontal line (W/P)_floor.
Compare the drop in employment when the wage is stuck at (W/P)_floor versus if the wage could fall to the new intersection.

options_template.text: The real wage falls immediately to clear the market, keeping employment constant at L*.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Flexible-Wage Assumption): Because the real wage is held rigid at (W/P)_floor, it cannot fall to absorb the negative shock.

options_template.text: The horizontal gap L_S − L_D shrinks because fewer firms are hiring.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Direction Error): A leftward shift of L_D lowers L_D at the fixed wage floor while L_S stays unchanged, widening L_S − L_D.

options_template.text: The labor supply curve shifts leftward by the exact same distance, leaving unemployment unchanged.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Confounded Curve Shift): A negative shock to firms' labor demand does not automatically shift labor supply leftward by an identical amount.

options_template.text: Employment falls sharply to the new L_D coordinate along (W/P)_floor and the excess labor supply (L_S − L_D) widens more than it would under flexible wages.
options_template.feedback: Correct. With (W/P)_floor fixed, the entire adjustment falls on quantities: L_D drops horizontally at the rigid wage, expanding unemployment far more than if real wages could fall.

questions.title: Recessionary Demand Shock on the Beveridge Curve
questions.prompt_template: On the Beveridge Curve diagram with the job vacancy rate (v) on the vertical axis and the unemployment rate (u) on the horizontal axis, how is a recession driven by falling aggregate demand depicted?

hints.text: During an aggregate-demand recession, do firms post more or fewer job openings, and does unemployment rise or fall?
Business-cycle demand shocks move the economy ALONG a stable Beveridge Curve rather than shifting it.

options_template.text: A downward-right movement along the existing Beveridge Curve (lower vacancy rate v, higher unemployment rate u).
options_template.feedback: Correct. Falling aggregate demand leads firms to freeze hiring (lower v) and lay off workers (higher u), tracing a downward-right movement along BC_0.

options_template.text: An upward-left movement along the existing Beveridge Curve (higher vacancy rate v, lower unemployment rate u).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Boom vs. Recession Reversal): Higher vacancies and lower unemployment represent an economic expansion, not a recession.

options_template.text: A parallel outward shift of the Beveridge Curve to BC_1 (higher u at the same vacancy rate v).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Movement vs. Shift Confusion): An outward shift reflects deteriorated matching efficiency or structural reallocation, whereas a pure demand recession moves along BC_0.

options_template.text: A parallel inward shift of the Beveridge Curve toward the origin.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Matching-Improvement Confusion): An inward shift indicates improved matching efficiency (fewer unemployed workers per vacancy), not a demand recession.

questions.title: Economic Expansion on the Beveridge Curve
questions.prompt_template: Suppose strong aggregate demand stimulates rapid hiring across the economy while labor-market matching efficiency remains unchanged. How does this expansion appear on the Beveridge Curve?

hints.text: Matching efficiency is unchanged, so the economy stays on the same Beveridge Curve.
In a boom, vacancies are abundant (high v) and unemployment is low (low u).

options_template.text: A downward-right movement along the existing Beveridge Curve.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Recession Direction Error): Moving downward-right means falling vacancies and rising unemployment, which characterizes a downturn.

options_template.text: An upward-left movement along the existing Beveridge Curve (higher vacancy rate v, lower unemployment rate u).
options_template.feedback: Correct. With constant matching efficiency, rising aggregate demand increases job openings (v) and draws down unemployment (u), moving upward-left along BC_0.

options_template.text: An outward shift of the Beveridge Curve so that both v and u rise simultaneously.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Shift Confusion): A pure aggregate demand expansion does not impair matching efficiency or raise unemployment.

options_template.text: A vertical drop in the vacancy rate with no change in unemployment.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Slope Neglect): Along the downward-sloping Beveridge Curve, an expansion raises v while simultaneously lowering u.

questions.title: Interpreting an Outward Shift of the Beveridge Curve (BC_0 → BC_1)
questions.prompt_template: On the Beveridge Curve diagram, the economy moves horizontally from point A on BC_0 to point C on BC_1, such that the job vacancy rate remains v_0 while the unemployment rate rises from u_A to u_C. What does this shift signify?

hints.text: Why would more workers remain unemployed even though firms are posting the exact same rate of job openings (v_0)?
Think about structural frictions: skill mismatches, geographic immobility, or sectoral reallocation.

options_template.text: A pure shortfall in aggregate demand with unchanged labor-market matching efficiency.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Movement vs. Shift Confusion): A pure demand shortfall lowers v as u rises (a movement along BC_0), rather than keeping v constant at a higher u.

options_template.text: An improvement in digital job-matching platforms that accelerates hiring.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Shift Direction Error): Faster job matching shifts the Beveridge Curve INWARD (lower u for any given v), not outward.

options_template.text: A deterioration in labor-market matching efficiency—such as increased skill mismatch, geographic immobility, or rapid sectoral reallocation.
options_template.feedback: Correct. An outward shift (higher u at the same vacancy rate v_0) signals that job seekers and unfilled openings are matching less efficiently, pushing the natural rate u* higher.

options_template.text: A decline in the Okun coefficient β below 1.0.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Model Conflation): The Okun coefficient links cyclical unemployment to the GDP output gap, not horizontal shifts of the (u, v) Beveridge Curve.

questions.title: Cause of an Inward Shift of the Beveridge Curve
questions.prompt_template: Which structural development would shift the entire Beveridge Curve INWARD toward the origin?

hints.text: An inward shift means a lower unemployment rate u for every given job vacancy rate v.
Look for a change that speeds up matching between job seekers and employers (raising the job-finding rate f).

options_template.text: Widespread adoption of effective job-matching platforms and portable occupational licensing across states, reducing search and mobility frictions.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Improving matching efficiency and geographic mobility allows vacancies to be filled faster, lowering u at any given v and shifting the Beveridge Curve inward.

options_template.text: A sudden wave of technological obsolescence that leaves displaced manufacturing workers lacking skills for open tech roles.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Direction Error): Skill mismatch impairs matching efficiency and shifts the Beveridge Curve OUTWARD, not inward.

options_template.text: A mild recession that reduces consumer spending and causes firms to cancel job postings.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Movement vs. Shift Confusion): A cyclical drop in aggregate spending causes a downward-right movement ALONG the existing curve rather than an inward shift.

options_template.text: A housing-market freeze that traps unemployed homeowners in declining regions unable to relocate for open jobs.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Direction Error): Geographic immobility worsens matching efficiency and shifts the Beveridge Curve OUTWARD.

questions.title: Interpreting Quadrants and Slope on the Okun's Law Graph
questions.prompt_template: In the Okun's Law graph plotting the percentage output gap (Y − Y*)/Y* on the vertical axis against cyclical slack (u − u*) on the horizontal axis, what does a point located in the second quadrant (top-left, where u − u* < 0 and (Y − Y*)/Y* > 0) represent?

hints.text: Check the signs of both axes in the top-left (second) quadrant: horizontal coordinate is negative, vertical coordinate is positive.
If u − u* < 0, then actual unemployment is below the natural rate; if (Y − Y*)/Y* > 0, actual GDP exceeds potential GDP.

options_template.text: A recessionary gap in which actual unemployment exceeds u* and real GDP falls short of potential output.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Quadrant Reversal): Recessionary slack (u − u* > 0, output gap < 0) lies in the fourth (bottom-right) quadrant, not the second quadrant.

options_template.text: Long-run full employment where cyclical unemployment and the output gap are both exactly zero.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Origin Confusion): Full employment corresponds to the origin (0, 0) where u = u* and Y = Y*.

options_template.text: A violation of Okun's Law because real GDP can never temporarily exceed potential real GDP Y*.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Hard-Ceiling Fallacy): Potential output Y* is sustainable capacity, not an absolute physical ceiling; during overheated expansions, Y can temporarily exceed Y* while u < u*.

options_template.text: An overheated expansion (positive output gap) where actual unemployment lies below the natural rate (u < u*) and real GDP temporarily exceeds potential output (Y > Y*).
options_template.feedback: Correct. Along the downward-sloping Okun line (slope −β), the second quadrant represents negative cyclical unemployment (u < u*) paired with a positive output gap (Y > Y*).

questions.title: Computing Headline U-3 and LFPR from Population Counts
questions.prompt_template: An economy has a Civilian Noninstitutional Population of P = 250.0 million, Employed workers E = 141.0 million, and Unemployed workers U = 9.0 million. What are the headline unemployment rate (U-3) and the labor force participation rate (LFPR)?

hints.text: First compute the labor force LF = E + U.
Then compute U-3 = (U / LF) × 100 and LFPR = (LF / P) × 100.

options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Population-Denominator Error): Dividing U (9.0M) by P (250.0M) gives 3.60%, but U-3 must divide U by LF = 150.0M.
Diagnostic fallacy (EPOP vs. LFPR Confusion): 141.0 / 250.0 = 56.40% is the Employment-to-Population Ratio (EPOP), not the Labor Force Participation Rate (LF / P = 60.00%).
Diagnostic fallacy (Double Denominator/Numerator Error): This divides U by P (giving 3.60%) and computes EPOP = E/P (56.40%) instead of LFPR.

questions.topic: Algebraic Identity Linking EPOP, LFPR, and U-3
questions.title: Deriving EPOP from LFPR and Headline U-3
questions.prompt_template: Suppose an economy has a Labor Force Participation Rate (LFPR) of 62.50% and a headline unemployment rate (U-3) of 4.00%. Using the algebraic identity linking these indicators, what is the Employment-to-Population Ratio (EPOP)?

hints.text: Use the exact identity EPOP = LFPR × (1 − U-3), expressed in proportions.
Since 4.00% of the labor force is unemployed, 96.00% of the labor force is employed.

options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Direct-Subtraction Error): Subtracting 4.00% directly from 62.50% ignores that U-3 is a fraction of LF, whereas LFPR is a fraction of P.
Diagnostic fallacy (Sign Error in Factor): Multiplying 62.50% by (1 + 0.04) = 65.00% erroneously adds unemployment instead of subtracting it; EPOP can never exceed LFPR.
Diagnostic fallacy (Unemployed-Share Error): Multiplying 62.50% by 0.04 gives U/P = 2.50% (the unemployed share of CNIP), rather than E/P = 60.00%.

questions.title: Computing U-6 Without Double-Counting Discouraged Workers
questions.prompt_template: In a national economy, Employed workers E = 114.0 million (of whom PT_econ = 4.0 million are part-time for economic reasons), Unemployed workers U = 6.0 million, and Marginally Attached workers M = 5.0 million (which includes D = 2.0 million discouraged workers). What is the broad underutilization rate U-6?

hints.text: First find LF = E + U = 120.0 million, and remember that discouraged workers (D) are already included inside M.
Apply U-6 = (U + M + PT_econ) / (LF + M) × 100.

options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Double-Counting Discouraged Workers): Adding both M (5.0M) and D (2.0M) yields 17.0 / 125.0 = 13.60%, double-counting the 2.0M discouraged workers already inside M.
Diagnostic fallacy (Denominator Omission Error): Dividing 15.0M by LF (120.0M) instead of LF + M (125.0M) yields 12.50% and omits NILF marginally attached workers from the denominator.
Diagnostic fallacy (U-5 Instead of U-6): Omitting PT_econ (4.0M) from the numerator gives (6.0 + 5.0) / 125.0 = 8.80%, which is U-5 rather than U-6.

questions.title: Calculating the New U-3 Rate After a Wave of Discouragement
questions.prompt_template: An economy initially has E = 117.0 million employed workers and U = 8.0 million unemployed workers (so LF = 125.0 million and initial U-3 = 6.40%). If 5.0 million unemployed workers become discouraged and stop actively searching while employment stays constant at 117.0 million, what is the new headline U-3 rate?

hints.text: Subtract 5.0 million from BOTH U and LF because discouraged workers exit the labor force.
Compute U-3_new = U_new / LF_new × 100.

options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Fixed-Denominator Error): Dividing U_new (3.0M) by the old labor force (125.0M) gives 2.40%, forgetting that discouraged workers also leave the denominator LF.
Diagnostic fallacy (Addition-to-Unemployment Fallacy): Adding 5.0M to U instead of subtracting yields 13.0 / 125.0 = 10.40%; discouraged workers exit U rather than entering it.
Diagnostic fallacy (Invariance Assumption): Leaving U-3 unchanged ignores that subtracting 5.0M from both U and LF reduces the numerator proportionally much faster than the denominator.

questions.title: Computing the Post-Recovery (U-6 − U-3) Spread
questions.prompt_template: A regional economy has LF = 75.0 million, U = 3.0 million (U-3 = 4.00%), M = 5.0 million marginally attached workers, and initially PT_econ = 6.0 million involuntary part-time workers. Suppose employers restore full-time hours to 4.0 million of these workers (reducing PT_econ to 2.0 million) while LF, U, and M stay unchanged. What is the NEW underutilization spread (U-6 − U-3) in percentage points?

hints.text: Compute the new U-6 using PT_econ = 2.0 million and denominator LF + M = 80.0 million.
Then subtract headline U-3 (4.00%) from the new U-6 to find the spread.

options_template.text: 13.50 percentage points
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Pre-Recovery Calculation): Using initial PT_econ = 6.0M gives initial U-6 = 14.0/80.0 = 17.50% and an initial spread of 13.50 percentage points, ignoring the recovery.

options_template.text: 8.50 percentage points
options_template.feedback: Correct. New U-6 = (3.0 + 5.0 + 2.0) / (75.0 + 5.0) × 100 = (10.0 / 80.0) × 100 = 12.50%. Subtracting U-3 = 4.00% yields a new spread of 8.50 percentage points.

options_template.text: 12.50 percentage points
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Level vs. Spread Confusion): 12.50% is the new U-6 rate itself, not the spread (U-6 − U-3).

options_template.text: 5.00 percentage points
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Change vs. Spread Confusion): 5.00 percentage points is the drop in U-6 (from 17.50% to 12.50%), not the remaining spread between U-6 and U-3.

questions.title: Computing Negative Cyclical Unemployment in an Expansion
questions.prompt_template: During a tight economic expansion, actual unemployment is u = 3.6%, frictional unemployment is u_f = 2.5%, and structural unemployment is u_s = 1.8%. What is the cyclical unemployment rate (u_c)?

hints.text: First compute the natural rate of unemployment: u* = u_f + u_s.
Then apply u_c = u − u*, paying close attention to the algebraic sign.

options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Sign Reversal): Computing u* − u gives +0.7%, which reverses the sign; when actual u is below u*, cyclical unemployment is negative.
Diagnostic fallacy (Omitting Structural Unemployment): Subtracting only u_f from u (3.6% − 2.5% = +1.1%) omits structural unemployment u_s from the natural rate u*.
Correct. u* = 2.5% + 1.8% = 4.3%, so u_c = u − u* = 3.6% − 4.3% = -0.7%, signaling an overheated labor market.
Diagnostic fallacy (Additive Error): Adding u and u* (3.6% + 4.3% = 7.9%) instead of taking their difference misapplies the decomposition identity u = u* + u_c.

questions.title: Calculating the Steady-State Natural Rate from Job Flows
questions.prompt_template: In a dynamic labor market with a constant labor force, the monthly job separation rate is s = 1.8% (0.018) and the monthly job-finding rate is f = 28.2% (0.282). What is the steady-state natural rate of unemployment u*?

hints.text: In steady state, inflows into unemployment equal outflows: s(1 − u*) = f u*.
Solve for u* using the Markov steady-state formula u* = s / (s + f).

options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Employment-Rate Inversion): Computing f / (s + f) = 0.282 / 0.300 = 94.00% gives the steady-state employment share (1 − u*), not the unemployment rate u*.
Diagnostic fallacy (Sum-of-Flows Error): Adding s + f = 1.8% + 28.2% = 30.00% computes the denominator of the flow formula rather than the steady-state unemployment rate.
Diagnostic fallacy (Flow vs. Stock Confusion): 1.80% is the monthly separation rate s (an inflow rate), not the steady-state unemployment stock u*.

questions.topic: Algebraic Wage Floor and Structural Unemployment
questions.title: Quantifying Structural Unemployment Under a Binding Real Wage Floor
questions.prompt_template: Suppose an aggregate labor market is described by labor demand L_D = 120 − 4(W/P) and labor supply L_S = 20 + 6(W/P), where L is in millions of workers and W/P is the real hourly wage. If a binding wage floor is imposed at W/P = 13, how many millions of workers are structurally unemployed?

hints.text: Substitute W/P = 13 into both L_D and L_S (note that equilibrium is W/P* = 10, L* = 80M, so 13 is binding).
Structural unemployment equals the excess labor supply L_S − L_D at the binding floor.

options_template.text: 12 million workers
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Jobs-Lost-Only Error): L* − L_D = 80 − 68 = 12 million counts only displaced workers and ignores the 18 million new job seekers attracted by the higher wage.

options_template.text: 18 million workers
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (New-Entrants-Only Error): L_S − L* = 98 − 80 = 18 million counts only new labor supply entrants and ignores the 12 million jobs cut by firms.

options_template.text: 68 million workers
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Employment vs. Unemployment Confusion): L_D = 120 − 4(13) = 68 million is the number of workers EMPLOYED at the wage floor, not structurally unemployed.

options_template.text: 30 million workers
options_template.feedback: Correct. At W/P = 13, L_D = 120 − 52 = 68M and L_S = 20 + 78 = 98M, yielding structural unemployment of L_S − L_D = 98 − 68 = 30 million workers.

questions.title: Calculating Actual Real GDP from an Okun's Law Recessionary Gap
questions.prompt_template: An economy has potential real GDP Y* = $24.0 trillion, a natural rate of unemployment u* = 4.50%, an actual unemployment rate u = 6.25%, and an Okun coefficient β = 2.0. What is actual real GDP (Y)?

hints.text: First find cyclical unemployment u − u* = 6.25% − 4.50% = +1.75% (0.0175), then multiply by −β = −2.0 for the percentage output gap.
Multiply the percentage output gap by Y* = $24.0 trillion to get Y − Y*, then solve for Y.

options_template.text: $23.58 trillion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Omitting Okun's β): Using a 1-for-1 gap of −1.75% gives −$0.42 trillion and $23.58 trillion, forgetting to multiply by β = 2.0.

options_template.text: $23.16 trillion
options_template.feedback: Correct. The output gap is −2.0 × 0.0175 = −3.50%, giving a dollar shortfall of −0.035 × $24.0T = −$0.84T and actual real GDP Y = $24.0T − $0.84T = $23.16 trillion.

options_template.text: $24.84 trillion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Sign Error): Adding +$0.84 trillion instead of subtracting it produces $24.84 trillion; when u > u*, actual GDP must lie BELOW potential Y*.

options_template.text: $21.00 trillion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Total vs. Cyclical Unemployment Error): Multiplying −2.0 by total u (6.25%) instead of cyclical slack (u − u* = 1.75%) yields a −12.5% gap (−$3.0T) and $21.00 trillion.

questions.title: Solving for Actual Unemployment from a Positive Output Gap
questions.prompt_template: Suppose potential real GDP is Y* = $20.0 trillion, actual real GDP is Y = $20.6 trillion, the natural rate of unemployment is u* = 4.50%, and the Okun coefficient is β = 2.0. According to Okun's Law, what is the actual unemployment rate (u)?

hints.text: Compute the percentage output gap (Y − Y*) / Y* = ($20.6T − $20.0T) / $20.0T = +3.00%.
Substitute into +3.00% = −2.0(u − 4.50%) and solve for u.

options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Sign Error): Adding 1.50% to u* gives 6.00%, which implies a recessionary gap rather than an expansion where Y > Y*.
Diagnostic fallacy (Omitting Division by β): Subtracting the full +3.00% output gap from 4.50% gives 1.50%, forgetting to divide by β = 2.0.
Diagnostic fallacy (Dollar-vs.-Percent Confusion): Subtracting the $0.6 trillion dollar gap directly from 4.50% mixes trillions of dollars with percentage points.

questions.title: Predicting the Change in Unemployment from Real GDP Growth
questions.prompt_template: An economy has trend potential GDP growth g_{Y*} = 2.5% per year and an Okun coefficient β = 2.0. If actual real GDP grows by g_Y = 0.9% over the year, by how many percentage points does the unemployment rate change (Δu)?

hints.text: Use the growth-rate form of Okun's Law: g_Y − g_{Y*} = −β Δu.
Because actual growth (0.9%) is slower than potential trend growth (2.5%), unemployment must rise (Δu > 0).

options_template.text: -0.80 percentage points
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Sign Reversal): Falling below trend potential growth pushes unemployment UP, not down; dropping the minus sign in −β Δu flips the direction.

options_template.text: +1.60 percentage points
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Omitting Division by β): Reporting g_{Y*} − g_Y = +1.60 forgets to divide the growth shortfall by β = 2.0.

options_template.text: +0.80 percentage points
options_template.feedback: Correct. Substituting into g_Y − g_{Y*} = −β Δu gives 0.9% − 2.5% = −1.6% = −2.0 Δu, so Δu = +0.80 percentage points.

options_template.text: +3.20 percentage points
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Multiplying Instead of Dividing by β): Multiplying 1.6% by 2.0 instead of dividing yields +3.20 percentage points.

questions.title: Required Real GDP Growth to Lower Unemployment
questions.prompt_template: If trend potential GDP growth is g_{Y*} = 2.2% per year and the Okun coefficient is β = 2.0, what annual real GDP growth rate (g_Y) is required to reduce the unemployment rate by 0.60 percentage points (Δu = −0.60%) over one year?

hints.text: Rearrange g_Y − g_{Y*} = −β Δu to solve for g_Y = g_{Y*} − β Δu.
Remember that reducing unemployment requires growing FASTER than potential trend growth g_{Y*}.

options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Sign Error): Computing 2.2% − 1.2% = 1.00% ignores the double negative in −β(−0.60%); growing slower than 2.2% would raise unemployment.
Diagnostic fallacy (Omitting Okun's β): Adding 0.60% directly to 2.2% gives 2.80%, forgetting that each 1-percentage-point drop in u requires β = 2.0 percentage points of above-trend growth.
Diagnostic fallacy (Omitting Trend Growth g_{Y*}): 1.20% is only the extra above-trend growth (−β Δu); without adding g_{Y*} = 2.2%, unemployment would actually rise.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Reconciling Rising CES Payrolls with a Rising CPS Unemployment Rate
questions.prompt_template: During the early phase of an economic recovery, the BLS reports that CES nonfarm payroll employment increased by 250,000 jobs in the same month that the CPS headline unemployment rate (U-3) ticked upward from 5.2% to 5.4%. Which explanation best reconciles both accurate statistics?

hints.text: Think about how improving job prospects affect previously discouraged workers (NILF → U) and multiple jobholders.
Both surveys measure different margins and are fully consistent when labor force re-entry outpaces immediate hiring.

options_template.text: Improving job prospects drew previously discouraged and marginally attached workers back into active job search (NILF → U) faster than they were hired, and/or existing workers took second payroll jobs.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Re-entrants from NILF raise both U and LF (pushing U-3 up temporarily), while multiple jobholders boost CES payroll counts even though CPS counts each person only once.

options_template.text: One of the two BLS surveys must contain a statistical error because payroll employment and U-3 can never rise in the same month.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Monotonicity Myth): Because CPS and CES differ in labor-force entry dynamics and multiple-job counting, U-3 and payrolls frequently rise together during early recoveries.

options_template.text: Workers who switched from full-time to involuntary part-time schedules were automatically counted as unemployed in U-3.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (U-3 vs. U-6 Confusion): Involuntary part-time workers remain in Employed (E) and do not raise U-3.

options_template.text: A wave of retirees left the labor force, which mechanically increased both CES payrolls and CPS U-3.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Retirement Flow Error): Retirees exiting employment reduce CES payrolls rather than increasing them, and retiring from NILF does not affect U-3.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Using Prime-Age EPOP (LNS12300060) to Interpret Secular Declines in CIVPART
questions.prompt_template: Between 2000 and 2015, the U.S. Labor Force Participation Rate (FRED: CIVPART) fell from roughly 67.3% to 62.4%. Why do macroeconomists cross-check CIVPART against the Prime-Age Employment-to-Population Ratio (ages 25–54, FRED: LNS12300060) when assessing cyclical labor market health?

hints.text: What non-cyclical demographic forces pulled overall CIVPART downward between 2000 and 2015?
Restricting the ratio to ages 25–54 removes two major age-driven participation shifts.

options_template.text: Because CIVPART excludes unemployed workers, whereas Prime-Age EPOP includes both employed and unemployed workers.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Formula Inversion): CIVPART = (E + U)/P includes unemployed workers, whereas EPOP = E/P measures only the employed share.

options_template.text: Because Prime-Age EPOP is derived from the CES Establishment Survey rather than the CPS Household Survey.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Survey Misattribution): Both CIVPART and Prime-Age EPOP (LNS12300060) are derived from the CPS Household Survey.

options_template.text: Because Prime-Age EPOP strips out secular population aging (Baby Boom retirements) and increased youth college enrollment, as well as boundary shifts between U and NILF.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Focusing on ages 25–54 isolates core working-age employment from demographic retirement waves, youth schooling trends, and discouraged-worker flows between U and NILF.

options_template.text: Because CIVPART is not seasonally adjusted, whereas Prime-Age EPOP removes all cyclical business-cycle fluctuations.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Cyclicality Error): Prime-Age EPOP is highly sensitive to business cycles—that is precisely why economists use it to gauge cyclical slack cleanly.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Why EMRATIO Complemented UNRATE During the Spring 2020 Pandemic Shock
questions.prompt_template: During the onset of the COVID-19 shock in spring 2020, U.S. CIVPART plunged by roughly 3 percentage points. Why did relying solely on headline UNRATE risk understating the true loss of jobs during lockdowns, and why was EMRATIO an essential cross-check?

hints.text: Remember the CPS active-search requirement: what happens if lockdowns prevent displaced workers from searching for jobs?
Compare how EMRATIO = E / P behaves versus UNRATE = U / (E + U) when displaced workers land in NILF.

options_template.text: Lockdowns caused self-employed workers to be dropped from the CPS entirely, while EMRATIO counted them twice.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Survey Coverage Error): The CPS always includes self-employed workers in E and counts each person once.

options_template.text: Lockdowns prevented millions of displaced workers from conducting active job searches, temporarily classifying them as NILF rather than U; EMRATIO captured the full employment drop directly in E/P.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Because workers unable to search actively fell into NILF instead of U, UNRATE understated total joblessness; EMRATIO = E/P directly measured the share of the working-age population still holding jobs.

options_template.text: Headline UNRATE only tracks involuntary part-time workers, whereas EMRATIO tracks full-time workers.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Metric Confusion): UNRATE tracks unemployed workers (U/LF), and EMRATIO includes all employed workers (full-time and part-time) divided by CNIP.

options_template.text: A drop in CIVPART mechanically pushes UNRATE upward even when employment stays constant.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Direction Error): When workers exit the labor force into NILF, CIVPART falls and UNRATE is depressed downward, not pushed upward.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Interpreting the U6RATE − UNRATE Spread Across Business Cycles
questions.prompt_template: In October 2009 (following the Great Recession), U-3 peaked at 10.0% while U-6 reached 17.1% (a 7.1-percentage-point spread). During the tight labor market of 2022–2023, U-3 fell to 3.4% and U-6 fell to 6.5% (a 3.1-percentage-point spread). What economic mechanism explains why the U-6 minus U-3 spread compressed by 4.0 percentage points in 2022–2023?

hints.text: Identify the two groups that separate U-6 from U-3: marginally attached workers (M) and involuntary part-time workers (PT_econ).
How do firms adjust worker hours and how do marginally attached workers behave when labor markets become extremely tight?

options_template.text: The BLS changed the definition of U-6 in 2022 to exclude discouraged workers.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Definition-Change Myth): The BLS definition of U-6 remained unchanged; the narrower spread reflected genuine labor market tightening.

options_template.text: Millions of workers voluntarily chose part-time schedules in 2022–2023, which directly reduced the U-6 numerator.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Voluntary Part-Time Confusion): Voluntary part-time workers are never included in PT_econ or U-6, so switching to voluntary part-time does not explain the cyclical compression.

options_template.text: Higher inflation automatically reduces U-6 faster than U-3 through nominal wage indexing.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Nominal-Metric Confusion): Both U-3 and U-6 are purely quantity-based headcount ratios with no nominal price or wage terms.

options_template.text: In a tight labor market, firms converted involuntary part-time schedules into full-time positions to retain staff and previously marginally attached workers were drawn back into jobs, shrinking both PT_econ and M.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Because the spread reflects work-hour rationing (PT_econ) and latent labor supply (M), intense employer demand in 2022–2023 sharply reduced both components.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.topic: Critical Evaluation of Headline Unemployment Claims
questions.title: Auditing a Policymaker's Claim About Falling Headline U-3
questions.prompt_template: During the second year of a severe recession, a government spokesperson points out that headline U-3 fell from 8.4% to 7.8% over the past quarter and claims this proves businesses are rapidly hiring new workers. Which set of companion indicators would most directly REFUTE the spokesperson's claim?

hints.text: If U-3 fell because of discouragement rather than hiring, what should happen to EPOP, LFPR, and U-6?
Genuine hiring raises EPOP; discouraged-worker exits leave EPOP flat (or falling) while LFPR drops and U-6 stays elevated.

options_template.text: EPOP remained flat, LFPR fell sharply, and U-6 stayed unchanged at 15.2%.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Flat EPOP proves no net employment growth occurred; falling LFPR alongside unchanged U-6 confirms that U-3 dropped solely because unemployed workers became discouraged and moved from U to M.

options_template.text: EPOP rose sharply, LFPR increased, and U-6 fell from 15.2% to 13.8%.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Evidence Reversal): Rising EPOP, rising LFPR, and falling U-6 would actually CONFIRM genuine hiring and broad labor market improvement.

options_template.text: CES nonfarm payrolls rose by 300,000 per month and involuntary part-time work declined.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Evidence Reversal): Strong payroll gains and falling PT_econ support—rather than refute—the claim of a hiring rebound.

options_template.text: The job vacancy rate (v) surged while U-1 (long-term unemployment) fell sharply.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Evidence Reversal): Rising vacancies and declining long-term joblessness indicate strengthening labor demand, not artificial labor-force exit.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Evaluating the Macroeconomic Trade-Off of Generous Unemployment Insurance
questions.prompt_template: Economists note that expanding the generosity and duration of Unemployment Insurance (UI) involves an important macroeconomic trade-off. Which statement accurately captures BOTH sides of this trade-off?

hints.text: Consider both the benefit to households/match quality and the incentive effect on search duration.
Does UI primarily affect cyclical demand collapse or the opportunity cost of search (frictional unemployment u_f)?

options_template.text: UI eliminates structural skill mismatches permanently, but it causes EPOP to rise above 100%.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Impossible Bound & Mechanism Error): UI provides income replacement rather than technical retraining, and EPOP cannot exceed 100%.

options_template.text: UI lowers frictional unemployment by forcing workers to accept the very first job offer they receive, while raising cyclical unemployment.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Incentive Inversion): More generous UI reduces urgency to accept an unsuitable first offer, lengthening rather than shortening average search spells.

options_template.text: UI cushions household consumption and enables workers to wait for better-fitting job matches, but it lowers the opportunity cost of remaining unemployed and slightly raises frictional unemployment (u_f) and u*.
options_template.feedback: Correct. UI stabilizes consumption and improves match quality, while modestly reducing search intensity and nudging u_f and the natural rate u* upward.

options_template.text: UI has zero effect on worker search behavior because CPS respondents must hide UI benefits to remain in U.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Incentive Denial & CPS Myth): UI replacement rates directly alter the opportunity cost of search, and CPS classification does not depend on hiding UI benefits.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.topic: Demographic Composition and the Natural Rate
questions.title: How Workforce Aging Influenced the U.S. Natural Rate (u*) Since the 1980s
questions.prompt_template: Since the 1980s, the average age of the U.S. labor force has risen substantially as the Baby Boom generation matured. Through which channel did this demographic shift exert secular DOWNWARD pressure on the natural rate of unemployment (u*)?

hints.text: Compare the monthly job-separation rate (s) of younger workers sampling careers versus older, established workers.
Recall from the Markov steady-state relation u* = s / (s + f) how a lower separation rate s affects u*.

options_template.text: Older workers are excluded from the Civilian Noninstitutional Population after age 55, mechanically lowering u*.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (CNIP Age-Cap Myth): There is no upper age limit on the CNIP; anyone aged 16 or older who is civilian and noninstitutionalized is included.

options_template.text: Older workers exhibit lower job-separation rates (s) than younger workers who frequently sample careers, reducing frictional turnover and exerting downward pressure on u*.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Because younger workers change jobs more frequently (higher s), an aging workforce reduces aggregate separation rates and puts secular downward pressure on u*.

options_template.text: Older workers are legally exempt from minimum wage laws, eliminating structural unemployment.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Institutional Myth): Minimum wage laws apply across age groups and do not exempt older workers.

options_template.text: Workforce aging raises the Okun coefficient β from 2.0 to 4.0, which lowers frictional unemployment.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Model Conflation): Okun's β links cyclical unemployment to the output gap and does not govern the demographic trend in u*.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Why Policy Cannot Sustainably Hold Actual Unemployment Below u*
questions.prompt_template: Suppose a central bank attempts to keep actual unemployment permanently at 2.5% when the economy's natural rate of unemployment (NAIRU) is u* = 4.5%. What macroeconomic consequence does the chapter identify as the primary constraint on this policy?

hints.text: Recall why u* is called the Non-Accelerating Inflation Rate of Unemployment (NAIRU).
When u < u*, labor markets are overheated and vacancies are hard to fill.

options_template.text: Actual real GDP will collapse below potential output Y* because frictional unemployment is negative.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Sign & Output Confusion): Frictional unemployment cannot be negative, and u < u* corresponds to Y > Y* (a positive output gap), not a GDP collapse.

options_template.text: The U-6 rate will fall below the U-3 rate as employers eliminate all part-time positions.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Algebraic Impossibility): Because M ≥ 0 and PT_econ ≥ 0 (with U < LF), U-6 can never fall below U-3.

options_template.text: The labor force participation rate will immediately drop to zero as workers become discouraged.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Boom vs. Bust Confusion): Tight labor markets with u < u* encourage labor force entry rather than discouragement.

options_template.text: Persistent labor shortages force employers to bid up wages, generating upward wage-price inflation pressure rather than sustainable long-run output gains.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Holding u persistently below NAIRU (u*) overheats the labor market, triggering accelerating wage and price inflation without permanently expanding potential output Y*.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Matching Policy Tools to Cyclical vs. Structural Unemployment
questions.prompt_template: An economy has actual unemployment u = 6.2%, an estimated natural rate u* = 6.0% (up from 4.5% a decade earlier), and an outward-shifted Beveridge Curve with historically high unfilled job vacancies. Which policy mix best addresses the primary source of joblessness?

hints.text: First check cyclical unemployment u_c = u − u* = +0.2%: is this primarily a cyclical demand problem or a structural matching problem?
High vacancies alongside high unemployment point to structural mismatch rather than insufficient aggregate spending.

options_template.text: Targeted supply-side policies—such as workforce retraining, job-matching platforms, and reduced geographic/licensing barriers—to lower structural unemployment and shift the Beveridge Curve inward.
options_template.feedback: Correct. With u ≈ u* and high vacancies on an outward-shifted Beveridge Curve, joblessness is predominantly structural; retraining and matching improvements raise f and lower u*.

options_template.text: Massive expansionary fiscal and monetary stimulus to boost aggregate demand, since cyclical unemployment is the dominant problem.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Misdiagnosed Demand Problem): Cyclical slack is tiny (u_c = 0.2%); aggressive demand stimulus when vacancies are already high would mainly fuel wage-price inflation.

options_template.text: Raising the statutory minimum wage substantially above equilibrium to increase workers' purchasing power and close the Beveridge shift.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Wage-Floor Backfire): Pushing a binding wage floor further above equilibrium widens structural unemployment (L_S − L_D) rather than resolving matching frictions.

options_template.text: Cutting the CES Establishment Survey sample size so fewer unfilled vacancies are reported.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Measurement-Manipulation Fallacy): Altering survey sampling does not fix underlying skill mismatches, and vacancies are measured by JOLTS, not CES.
