questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Interpreting the 2021–2024 U.S. Beveridge Curve and 'Soft Landing'
questions.prompt_template: In 2021–2022, U.S. JOLTS job openings surged past 12.0 million (a vacancy rate above 7%) while unemployment remained near 3.6%–4.0%, shifting the Beveridge Curve outward. Between 2022 and 2024, Federal Reserve tightening cooled the vacancy rate back toward 4.5% with only a modest rise in unemployment. How do macroeconomists interpret this 2022–2024 trajectory?

hints.text: Compare a steep drop in v with a small rise in u against a standard movement down a flat Beveridge Curve.
Remember what caused the 2021–2022 outward shift: rapid post-pandemic sectoral reallocation and remote-work dispersion.

options_template.text: A permanent structural breakdown in which the natural rate of unemployment rose above 10%.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Historical Contradiction): Unemployment rose only modestly as vacancies fell, moving the economy back toward normal matching rather than toward 10% joblessness.

options_template.text: Evidence that Okun's Law no longer holds whenever JOLTS openings exceed 10 million.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Model Conflation): The 2022–2024 episode illustrates Beveridge Curve normalization (inward return from BC_1 toward BC_0), not a failure of Okun's Law.

options_template.text: An inward normalization of the Beveridge Curve back toward BC_0—cooling excess vacancy demand as post-pandemic reallocation frictions eased, achieving a 'soft landing' without a severe recession.
options_template.feedback: Correct. As pandemic reallocation frictions subsided and Fed tightening cooled excess vacancies, the economy moved steeply back inward toward BC_0 without triggering a sharp jump in unemployment.

options_template.text: A purely seasonal graduation wave that reversed itself every June.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Scale & Seasonal Error): JOLTS and UNRATE are seasonally adjusted, and the 2021–2024 shift spanned multiple years driven by pandemic reallocation and monetary policy.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Why Okun's Coefficient (β ≈ 2.0) Exceeds 1.0
questions.prompt_template: Empirically, a 1-percentage-point rise in U.S. cyclical unemployment (u − u*) is associated with roughly a 2.0% decline in real GDP below potential (β ≈ 2.0), rather than a 1.0% decline. Why does the percentage output loss exceed the percentage-point rise in unemployment?

hints.text: Think about what else happens to labor utilization and capital during a recession besides layoffs.
Consider average weekly hours (overtime), labor force participation, and factory capacity utilization.

options_template.text: Because the BLS double-counts every laid-off worker in both the CPS and CES surveys when calculating real GDP.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Accounting Myth): Real GDP is measured independently in the National Income and Product Accounts and does not double-count CPS and CES employment.

options_template.text: Because recessions simultaneously reduce overtime and average hours worked, push discouraged workers out of the labor force, and leave physical capital and factory capacity underutilized.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Beyond the 1-for-1 headcount drop in employment, intensive-margin hour cuts, labor-force exits, and idle machinery amplify the GDP shortfall to roughly 2% per 1-percentage-point rise in u.

options_template.text: Because laid-off workers are always twice as productive as employed workers.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Productivity Myth): Recessions do not selectively lay off workers with double average productivity; the amplification stems from hours, participation, and capital utilization.

options_template.text: Because inflation always rises by 2% during recessions, shrinking real GDP automatically.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Recessionary-Inflation Confusion): Real GDP is already adjusted for price changes, and demand-driven recessions typically exert downward—not upward—pressure on inflation.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Explaining Rising Unemployment During Positive Real GDP Growth
questions.prompt_template: Following a recession, real GDP begins growing at +1.4% per year while trend potential GDP growth is g_{Y*} = 2.4% per year. A news commentator expresses surprise that the unemployment rate rose over the year despite positive GDP growth. How does growth-rate Okun's Law explain this outcome?

hints.text: Recall g_Y − g_{Y*} = −β Δu: what growth rate is required just to keep Δu = 0?
Even when output expands, growing labor force and productivity mean potential output grows by g_{Y*} every year.

options_template.text: Unemployment always rises during positive GDP growth because Okun's coefficient β is positive.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Misreading the Minus Sign): In g_Y − g_{Y*} = −β Δu, unemployment falls (Δu < 0) whenever actual growth g_Y EXCEEDS trend potential growth g_{Y*}.

options_template.text: Positive real GDP growth can only lower U-6, never headline U-3.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Metric Misconception): Above-trend real GDP growth lowers both U-3 and U-6; here, growth is simply too slow relative to g_{Y*}.

options_template.text: The unemployment rate rose only because the Okun coefficient turned negative during the recovery.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Parameter-Flip Myth): β remains positive; the rise in u follows directly from g_Y < g_{Y*}.

options_template.text: Because real GDP must grow at the trend potential rate (2.4%) merely to absorb productivity and labor force growth and keep Δu = 0; positive growth below 2.4% is too slow to prevent unemployment from rising.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Under g_Y − g_{Y*} = −β Δu, positive growth of 1.4% still falls 1.0 percentage point short of trend growth (2.4%), pushing unemployment up by +0.50 percentage points (with β = 2.0).
